description: Toy Box Friends G2-12 (grade 2): the quarter is worth 25 cents, four quarters make one dollar (the Dollar Grid), count by 25s, and count mixed coins starting with the coin worth the most.

youtube.title: Quarters to a Dollar! Counting Coins for Kids | Grade 2 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Robo wants to ride the Big Loop train, and the ride costs one dollar. His jar has 13 coins, so is that 13 cents? No way! Cat shows that coins are worth different amounts: penny 1 cent, nickel 5 cents, dime 10 cents and the new coin, the quarter, 25 cents. The little dime is worth more than the big nickel, so size does not tell value. On the Dollar Grid of 100 squares, each quarter covers 25 squares and four quarters fill the whole dollar. We count by 25s on the Coin Ladder, sort coins and count the biggest value first, count Robo's jar to exactly one dollar, and check Dog's ticket piles.

For second graders (CCSS 2.MD.C.8: solve problems with dollars and coins).

Try at home with a grown-up: sort a handful of play coins into quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies, then count the quarters first. Safety: coins are small, so keep them away from babies, never put them in your mouth, and wash your hands after counting real coins.

do.text: Quarters to a Dollar
All aboard the Big Loop! One ride costs one dollar.
I've been saving my coins in this jar. Let's tip them out.
One, two, three... 13 coins. That's 13 cents. Not enough!
Wait. Coins are not all worth one cent. Let's count them properly.
Really? Then my jar might be enough. Let's find out!
Meet the coins. A penny is worth one cent.
penny
A nickel is worth five cents.
nickel
A dime is worth ten cents.
dime
And here is a new coin. The quarter. A quarter is worth 25 cents!
quarter = 25¢
The quarter is the biggest of the four coins.
Fun fact! The dime and the quarter have tiny ridges around the edge.
The penny and the nickel are smooth. You can tell them apart by touch.
Easy! Bigger coins are worth more. So the nickel beats the dime.
Which is worth more?
Not so fast! The little dime is worth ten cents. The big nickel is only five.
The dime is the smallest, thinnest coin, but it's worth more. Size doesn't tell value.
Size does not tell value
Penny one cent, nickel five, dime ten, quarter 25. Got it!
But why is it called a quarter? Let's build the Dollar Grid.
One dollar is worth 100 cents. This grid has 100 squares, one for every cent.
A quarter is worth 25 cents, so it covers 25 squares.
Two quarters cover 50 squares.
What comes after 50 when we count quarters?
75! Three quarters cover 75 squares.
And the fourth quarter fills the whole grid. 100 cents!
Four quarters make one dollar. Each quarter is one fourth of a dollar.
4 quarters = 100¢ = $1
Four equal parts are quarters, just like the four parts of a pizza.
Now let's count by 25s on the Coin Ladder.
Each quarter is one big leap of 25.
25, 50, 75, 100. Four leaps, one dollar!
Our Small Loop ride costs 50 cents. How many quarters is that?
Two quarters. 25, 50.
The Tunnel Ride costs 75 cents.
Three quarters. 25, 50, 75.
Take a giant step for every quarter with me!
Here are four coins in a messy order. Let's count them.
One. 26. 31. 41. Phew, that was tricky.
Now let's sort them first, with the coin worth the most at the top.
Quarter first. 25. Then 35. 40. 41!
The same 41 cents, but the steps are much easier.
Start with the coin worth the most
Cat, your ticket costs 60 cents. Count these.
Quarters first. 25, 50. Then the dime makes 60!
Now a mix. What is the biggest coin here?
The quarter! 25. Then the dimes, 35, 45. The nickel, 50. Pennies, 51, 52, 53.
53 cents. Sorting first makes counting easy!
One quarter!
Twenty-five!
Twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five...
One whole dollar! Ride time, ride!
Four quarters!
One dollar!
Now my jar! 13 coins. Let's sort them, biggest value first.
Two quarters, three dimes, three nickels, five pennies. Count with me!
100 cents! One dollar from just 13 coins.
Yes! I can ride the Big Loop!
One dollar, thank you. Here is your ticket!
Ticket check! Which piles make one dollar? Count each one.
Pile A. Four quarters.
Pile B. Three quarters, two dimes and a nickel.
25, 50, 75. Then 85, 95. And the nickel makes 100!
Pile C. Three quarters and two dimes.
Is pile C a dollar?
25, 50, 75, 85, 95. Only 95 cents. Five cents short!
Which coin is missing?
A nickel! Five more cents makes 100.
Pile D. Ten dimes.
100 pennies make a dollar too. But that takes a long time to count!
Quiz time! How much is a quarter worth?
25 cents!
How much are three quarters?
One quarter, one dime and two pennies. How much?
How many quarters make one dollar?
Four quarters!
Which do you count first, a dime or a quarter?
The quarter, because it's worth the most.
Let's remember. A quarter is 25 cents. Four quarters make one dollar.
Sort first, and start with the coin worth the most. Size doesn't tell value.
Try it at home with a grown-up. Sort play coins, then count the quarters first.
Keep coins away from babies
Never put coins in your mouth, and wash your hands after counting.
All aboard the Big Loop!
Counted, checked, all aboard!
Bye, friends! Twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five, one whole dollar!
